title: Two Sum
understanding: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.
key_observation: Instead of a nested loop (brute force O(n^2)), we can use a hash map to keep track of numbers we have seen. For each number x, we just need to check if (target - x) already exists in the hash map.
brute_force: Use two nested loops. For every pair (i, j) where i != j, check if nums[i] + nums[j] == target. Time: O(n^2), Space: O(1).
optimized_approach: Initialize an empty hash map. Iterate through the array. For each element num at index i, calculate complement = target - num. If complement exists in the hash map, return [hashmap[complement], i]. Otherwise, add num -> i to the hash map.
time_complexity: O(n) because we traverse the array once. Each lookup in the hash map is O(1) average.
space_complexity: O(n) because in the worst case we store all n elements in the hash map.
common_mistakes: Returning the numbers themselves instead of their indices. Using the same element twice (e.g., if target=6 and array has a single 3 at index 0, returning [0, 0] is wrong). Not handling duplicate values properly.

title: Valid Parentheses
understanding: Given a string s containing only characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. Open brackets must be closed by the same type of brackets and must be closed in the correct order.
key_observation: A stack is the perfect data structure here. When we see an opening bracket, we push it. When we see a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opening bracket. If not, the string is invalid.
brute_force: Repeatedly scan and remove matched pairs until no more pairs can be removed. If the string becomes empty, it is valid. Time: O(n^2).
optimized_approach: Initialize an empty stack. Iterate through each character. If it is an opening bracket, push it onto the stack. If it is a closing bracket, check if stack is empty (return False) or if stack.top matches the closing bracket (pop it), else return False. At the end, return True only if stack is empty.
time_complexity: O(n) where n is the length of the string.
space_complexity: O(n) in the worst case (e.g., all opening brackets).
common_mistakes: Forgetting to check if the stack is empty when encountering a closing bracket. Forgetting to check if the stack is empty at the end. Not handling all three types of bracket pairs.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
understanding: Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i, find the maximum profit you can achieve. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day. If no profit is possible, return 0.
key_observation: We want to find the maximum (prices[j] - prices[i]) where j > i. We can do this in a single pass by tracking the minimum price seen so far and updating the maximum profit at each step.
brute_force: Try all pairs (i, j) where i < j. Time: O(n^2), Space: O(1).
optimized_approach: Initialize min_price = infinity and max_profit = 0. Iterate through prices. For each price, update min_price = min(min_price, price). Then update max_profit = max(max_profit, price - min_price). Return max_profit.
time_complexity: O(n) single pass through the array.
common_mistakes: Selling before buying (j must be > i). Returning a negative profit when no profitable transaction is possible (should return 0). Updating max_profit before updating min_price.

title: Valid Anagram
understanding: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram uses the same characters with the same frequency, just rearranged.
key_observation: If two strings are anagrams, sorting them both will produce the same result. Alternatively, the character frequency count of both strings must be identical.
brute_force: Sort both strings and compare. Time: O(n log n), Space: O(n).
optimized_approach: If lengths differ, return False immediately. Use a hash map (or array of size 26) to count character frequencies. Increment for characters in s, decrement for characters in t. If all counts are 0 at the end, they are anagrams.
time_complexity: O(n) where n is the length of the strings.
space_complexity: O(1) since the hash map contains at most 26 keys (lowercase English letters).
common_mistakes: Not checking if the lengths are equal first. Assuming the strings only contain lowercase letters when the problem may include uppercase or special characters.

title: Maximum Subarray
understanding: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray which has the largest sum and return its sum. (Kadane's algorithm problem)
key_observation: At every position, we have two choices: extend the current subarray by including the current element, or start a new subarray at the current element. We choose whichever gives a larger result. If the current running sum becomes negative, it is always better to restart from the current element.
brute_force: Try all O(n^2) subarrays and calculate their sum. Time: O(n^2) or O(n^3).
optimized_approach: Kadane's Algorithm: Initialize current_sum = nums[0] and max_sum = nums[0]. For each element from index 1 onwards: current_sum = max(nums[i], current_sum + nums[i]); max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum). Return max_sum.
common_mistakes: Initializing max_sum = 0, which fails when all numbers are negative. Not considering a subarray of just one element.

title: Merge Intervals
understanding: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.
key_observation: If we sort intervals by start time, overlapping intervals will always be adjacent. Two intervals overlap if the start of the second is <= the end of the first.
brute_force: Check every pair of intervals to see if they overlap and merge. Repeat until no more merges are possible. Very slow.
optimized_approach: Sort intervals by start time. Initialize result with the first interval. For each subsequent interval, if its start <= result[-1][1] (end of last merged interval), merge them by updating end = max(result[-1][1], current end). Otherwise, add it as a new interval.
time_complexity: O(n log n) due to sorting. Merging itself is O(n).
common_mistakes: Not sorting the intervals first. When merging, forgetting to take the maximum of the two end values (instead of the end of the second interval, which could be smaller).

title: Binary Search
understanding: Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, return the index if the target is found. If not, return -1. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
key_observation: Since the array is sorted, we can eliminate half the search space at each step by comparing the target to the middle element.
brute_force: Linear scan: check every element. Time: O(n).
optimized_approach: Use two pointers: left = 0, right = len(nums) - 1. While left <= right: mid = left + (right - left) // 2. If nums[mid] == target, return mid. If nums[mid] < target, left = mid + 1. Else right = mid - 1. Return -1.
time_complexity: O(log n) because we halve the search space every iteration.
space_complexity: O(1) iterative solution uses no extra space.
common_mistakes: Integer overflow when computing mid (use left + (right-left)//2 not (left+right)//2). Using left < right instead of left <= right, which misses a single-element array case. Off-by-one errors in the boundary updates.

title: Climbing Stairs
understanding: You are climbing a staircase that takes n steps to reach the top. Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
key_observation: This is essentially the Fibonacci sequence. To reach step n, you could have come from step n-1 (1 step) or step n-2 (2 steps). So ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
brute_force: Recursion without memoization: try all combinations. Time: O(2^n) - exponential.
optimized_approach: Dynamic Programming: dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i. dp[1] = 1, dp[2] = 2. For i from 3 to n: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. Return dp[n]. Can be optimized to O(1) space by keeping only the last two values.
space_complexity: O(1) if we only store the previous two values.
common_mistakes: Not handling base cases (n=1 or n=2). Using O(n) space when O(1) is achievable. Confusing index 0 and index 1 based DP arrays.

title: Linked List Cycle
category: Linked List / Two Pointers / Floyd's Algorithm
understanding: Given head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it. A cycle exists if some node can be reached again by continuously following the next pointer.
key_observation: Use Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm (slow and fast pointers). A slow pointer moves 1 step at a time. A fast pointer moves 2 steps. If there's a cycle, they will eventually meet. If there's no cycle, fast will reach null.
brute_force: Use a hash set to store visited nodes. If we visit a node we've seen before, there's a cycle. Time: O(n), Space: O(n).
optimized_approach: Initialize slow = head and fast = head. While fast and fast.next are not null: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next. If slow == fast at any point, there is a cycle. If we exit the loop, return False.
common_mistakes: Not checking fast and fast.next before accessing fast.next.next (causes null pointer exception). Returning the wrong boolean.

title: Reverse Linked List
understanding: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list.
key_observation: We need to change the next pointers of all nodes to point to the previous node. We can do this iteratively using three pointers (prev, curr, next) or recursively.
brute_force: Store all node values in an array, reverse the array, then overwrite node values. This doesn't truly reverse the list structure.
optimized_approach: Iterative: Initialize prev = None, curr = head. While curr is not None: next_node = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next_node. Return prev (new head). Recursive: base case if head is None or head.next is None return head. Else recursively reverse the rest and set head.next.next = head; head.next = None.
space_complexity: O(1) iterative, O(n) recursive due to call stack.
common_mistakes: Losing the reference to next node before updating the pointer. Forgetting to set head.next = None in recursive solution (creates a cycle).

title: Number of Islands
understanding: Given an m x n 2D binary grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count and return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
key_observation: Every time we find a '1' that hasn't been visited, we found a new island. We then use BFS or DFS to mark all connected land cells as visited so we don't count them again.
brute_force: No obvious brute force beyond the optimal approach itself.
optimized_approach: DFS approach: Iterate through each cell. If it is '1', increment island count, and recursively call DFS on its 4 neighbors (up, down, left, right), changing '1' to '0' (visited) as we go. BFS is similar using a queue.
time_complexity: O(m * n) where m and n are the dimensions of the grid.
space_complexity: O(m * n) for the recursion stack (DFS) or queue (BFS) in the worst case.
common_mistakes: Visiting already-visited cells again causing infinite loops. Not checking boundary conditions before accessing neighboring cells. Modifying the original grid (mark with '0' or use a separate visited array).

title: Coin Change
understanding: Given an integer array coins (coin denominations) and an integer amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount. If it cannot be made up, return -1. You have an infinite supply of each coin.
key_observation: This is a classic unbounded knapsack problem. dp[i] = fewest coins to make amount i. For each amount, try subtracting each coin and take the minimum.
brute_force: Recursion: try all combinations. Exponential time without memoization.
optimized_approach: Bottom-up DP: Initialize dp array of size (amount+1) with infinity. Set dp[0] = 0. For each amount from 1 to target: for each coin c <= current amount: dp[amount] = min(dp[amount], dp[amount - c] + 1). Return dp[amount] if != infinity else -1.
common_mistakes: Initializing dp[0] incorrectly. Using dp array of wrong size. Returning -1 for dp[amount] == 0 (which is only valid if amount == 0). Not checking if a solution exists.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
understanding: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence is derived from a string by deleting some (or no) characters without changing the order of the remaining characters.
key_observation: Use 2D DP. dp[i][j] = LCS of text1[:i] and text2[:j]. If text1[i-1] == text2[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. Otherwise, dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
brute_force: Generate all subsequences of both strings and find the longest common one. Exponential time.
optimized_approach: Build a 2D dp table of size (m+1) x (n+1) initialized to 0. Iterate i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1. Else dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). Return dp[m][n].
time_complexity: O(m * n) where m and n are lengths of the two strings.
space_complexity: O(m * n) for the DP table (can be optimized to O(min(m,n)) using two rows).
common_mistakes: Confusing subsequence with substring (substring must be contiguous, subsequence does not). Off-by-one errors in the DP table due to 1-indexed strings.
